questions.question: A transformer backward pass exceeds GPU memory because it retained many forward intermediates. What does gradient checkpointing change?
options: Move the model weights to the output layer and discard the residual stream.
Skip computing gradients for checkpointed layers during the backward pass.
Save every activation and recompute the optimizer state during forward.
Save segment inputs, then recompute intermediate activations during backward.
questions.explanation: Checkpointing stores selected segment inputs instead of every intermediate activation, then reruns the segment’s forward during backward to recreate values needed for derivatives. It trades extra computation for lower memory; it does not skip gradient computation.

questions.question: At long sequence length, which activation is the main target of selective checkpointing in the lesson?
options: FFN hidden activation, whose size grows quadratically with sequence length.
Attention softmax output, whose size grows quadratically with sequence length.
Optimizer state, whose size grows quadratically with sequence length.
Residual input, whose size grows quadratically with sequence length.
questions.explanation: The attention softmax tensor scales as B×L×L×heads, so its size grows quadratically with sequence length; FFN hidden activations grow linearly. Selective checkpointing targets that costly attention storage rather than the linear FFN tensor.

questions.question: For uniform-cost layers and L=64, what checkpoint spacing follows the lesson's sqrt(L) rule?
options: 4 layers per segment, since 64 divided by 16 is 4.
8 layers per segment, since sqrt(64)=8.
16 layers per segment, since 64 divided by 4 is 16.
64 layers per segment, since every layer is one segment.
questions.explanation: The classical uniform-layer rule uses segment spacing √L. For L=64, √64=8, so checkpoints are spaced every eight layers; 16 is a different divisor, not the square-root balance. This spacing balances stored checkpoints against recomputation.

questions.question: The lesson compares full-activation and checkpointed backward on the same toy model. What result should a correct recomputation implementation preserve?
options: Matching forward output and parameter gradients within the tested tolerance.
A different forward output but identical optimizer learning rate.
Matching activation memory but reversed parameter gradients.
A larger loss because recomputation changes the model function.
questions.explanation: Checkpointed execution recomputes the same layer functions, so its forward output and parameter gradients should match the full-activation run within numerical tolerance. The code verifies output equivalence and maximum gradient difference.

questions.question: A transformer already uses FlashAttention, which recomputes softmax efficiently. What checkpointing choice follows the lesson's guidance?
options: Checkpoint only the tokenizer because it has the largest activation tensor.
Avoid extra layer-level checkpointing around attention if it adds little memory benefit.
Replace FlashAttention with full attention before recomputing any layers.
Checkpoint every attention layer again because FlashAttention stores all softmax matrices.
questions.explanation: FlashAttention already recomputes softmax efficiently instead of retaining its full matrix, so wrapping the same attention in another layer-level checkpoint may save little additional memory while adding recompute work. Do not add it solely to save that softmax storage.

questions.question: A run is GPU-memory-bound, and CPU-GPU transfer bandwidth has headroom. When can activation offload be preferable to recomputation?
options: When the model has no backward pass and stores no activations.
When transfer cost is lower than the recompute cost and GPU memory is the bottleneck.
When the GPU is compute-bound and PCIe transfer is slower than recomputation.
When all activations are already small enough to fit without recomputation.
questions.explanation: Offload stores activations in CPU memory when GPU memory is the bottleneck and PCIe bandwidth has headroom. It is preferable when transfer time is below rematerialization cost; a slow transfer path makes recomputation better.
